title: Dhamaal 4 Blinks First: Ajay Devgn's Gang Sprints to July 10 to Clear the Decks for Nolan
excerpt: The OG Dhamaal boys unveiled their trailer off a 60-foot poster cascading down a waterfall, then quietly moved their release a week earlier — because even a treasure hunt knows when to get out of The Odyssey's way.
body:
The poster came down a waterfall.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=IG-eByZdz6Y

Not off a billboard, not unfurled on a stage — a 60-foot sheet of Dhamaal 4 cascading down a man-made cascade at Imagicaa while the cast stood beneath it, soaked in spray and spotlight. It is the most extra trailer launch Bollywood has thrown all year, and it is exactly the energy this franchise trades in: loud, shameless, allergic to subtlety. Subtle films do not announce themselves by drowning a poster.

And then, days later, the same makers did the most un-Dhamaal thing imaginable. They flinched.

Dhamaal 4 has moved up a week, from July 17 to July 10, and the reason is a single name that makes even Ajay Devgn's people do the math: Christopher Nolan. The Odyssey lands July 17 worldwide, advance booking on IMAX has already opened to a thunderous response, and exhibitors across India will hand Nolan every premium screen he wants. Going head-to-head would have meant fighting for the scraps. So the gang that spends three films chasing gold decided the smartest move was to grab the earlier weekend and run. Greed, but make it strategic.

"You might feel it's CG, but it's not — it was meant to be a 15-20 day schedule. Ajay Devgn managed to pull it off in JUST 3 days." — Arshad Warsi, on the trailer's cliff sequence

The trailer itself is pure franchise muscle memory. The OG boys are all back — Ajay Devgn, Arshad Warsi, Riteish Deshmukh, Jaaved Jaaferi, and Sanjay Mishra — chasing a mountain of gold across a landscape of double-crosses, with a fresh batch of co-conspirators in Esha Gupta, Sanjeeda Shaikh, Anjali Anand, Upendra Limaye, Vijay Patkar and Ravi Kishan. The premise is the only premise this series has ever needed: a fortune dangled in front of greedy idiots, and the comic carnage of watching them try to outrun each other to it. Directed by Indra Kumar, presented by T-Series in association with Devgn Films, it is selling nostalgia by the truckload — right down to nods to the 2007 original.

Nostalgia is the bet, and it is not a crazy one. Total Dhamaal was a genuine smash in 2019, and seven years is precisely the gap that turns a comedy people remember into a comedy people are desperate to relive. The cast knows the room they're playing. Newcomer Anjali Anand, who turns up in the trailer and the song 'Chatni', gushed about her co-star with the kind of warmth that doubles as promotion: "I have been a fan of Riteish and everything he has done, but now I'm a fan of the person as well. What a wonderful man to work with — our chemistry was very natural, and we were always laughing and joking." The music is doing its job too, with Guru Randhawa's 'Qeher' already out and pumping.

https://www.instagram.com/reel/DZfHMfdoqfb/

Here's the honest take: Dhamaal has never been cinema, and it has never pretended to be. It is a sugar rush — a treasure hunt with the depth of a WhatsApp forward and the timing of a stand-up set. Whether part four lands depends entirely on whether Indra Kumar still knows how to choreograph chaos, or whether the formula has finally curdled into noise. The trailer suggests the former. The waterfall suggests the makers are very, very nervous about the latter.

For the diaspora, the timing is almost a gift. Dhamaal 4 opens in cinemas worldwide on July 10, 2026, which means NRI audiences in the US, UK, Canada and the Gulf get a week of pure, uncomplicated Bollywood comedy on the big screen before Nolan swallows every IMAX in sight. Expect wide theatrical runs through the usual desi-friendly chains — AMC and Cinemark pockets in the US, Cineworld and Vue in the UK, Cineplex in Canada — and an OTT landing later in the year once the theatrical dust settles, almost certainly on a streaming home in the T-Series orbit.

It is a family film built for a Friday-night crowd that wants to laugh without thinking, in a language that tastes like home. Sometimes that is exactly the assignment. The gang got out of Nolan's way, planted its flag a week early, and dared the summer to ignore it. Whether the gold is real or fool's gold — well, that's the whole joke, isn't it.
